title: Suicidal Ideation -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Suicidal ideation refers to contemplation of self-harm or ending one’s life and is a critical mental health concern with potentially fatal consequences if not promptly recognized and managed. The condition may arise in individuals of any age or background and is commonly associated with psychiatric disorders, including depression, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and substance use disorders. Contributing risk factors include prior suicide attempts, chronic illness, psychosocial stressors, trauma, and limited social support. The pathophysiology involves complex interactions among neurobiological, genetic, and environmental factors influencing mood regulation and impulse control. Clinical manifestations range from passive death wishes to detailed suicidal plans.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Diagnosis relies on comprehensive psychiatric evaluation and risk assessment, often incorporating validated screening tools. Management emphasizes ensuring safety, addressing underlying psychiatric or medical conditions, and initiating pharmacologic and psychotherapeutic interventions. Complications include self-inflicted injury and completed suicide. Early identification and appropriate intervention significantly improve prognosis and reduce mortality associated with suicidal behavior.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to advance learners' competence in evaluating and managing suicidal ideation. title: Suicidal Ideation -- Introduction
content: Suicide comprises a significant public health issue in the U.S., with the age-adjusted suicide rate reaching 14.1 per 100,000 population in 2021. Increasing concern exists regarding deaths categorized as unintentional falls or poisonings, both of which have risen and may represent misclassified suicides. Between 2000 and 2018, the age-adjusted suicide rate increased by 36.7%. Among individuals aged 10 to 24 years, suicide stands as the 2nd leading cause of death. While the suicide rate in this demographic remained stable from 2001 to 2007, an upward trend persisted through 2021. [1]

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Introduction
content: Suicide rates in the U.S. demonstrate substantial demographic variation. In 2021, men had a suicide rate 4 times higher than women, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Individuals older than 85 years experienced the highest rates overall. Among adults aged 55 and older, the rate increased with age in men but decreased with age in women. [2] Pronounced racial disparities are evident, with the highest rate observed in American Indian and Alaska Native populations and the lowest among Asians. The rate in the former group is approximately 4 times higher than in the latter. [3] In 2021, the CDC reported that 12.3 million adults developed suicidal thoughts, 3.5 million made suicide plans, 1.7 million attempted suicide, and 48,183 died by suicide.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Introduction
content: Suicidal ideation is characterized by preoccupation with thoughts of self-harm or formulating plans for suicide. The intensity of ideation exists on a spectrum, beginning with a general desire to die without a concrete method, plan, or intent, and progressing to active suicidal ideation, which involves a detailed plan and determined intent to act. Suicidal ideation comprises a significant risk factor for both suicide attempts and deaths. [4] Although suicidal thoughts and behaviors are often considered a single concept, passive thinking, active planning, and actual behavior form a continuous spectrum. [5]

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Introduction
content: Some individuals attempt suicide without prior ideation, though underreporting due to stigma complicates accurate assessment. An illustrative analogy conceptualizes suicidal ideation as the substantial, unseen portion of an iceberg, with the act of suicide representing the visible tip. [6] This framework underscores the need for early identification and targeted intervention to prevent progression to suicide.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Introduction
content: Assessing suicidal ideation provides an early warning for potential suicidal acts and offers insights into the patient’s level of distress and specific needs. Only a subset of patients with suicidal ideation will attempt suicide. However, ideation accompanied by intention and a specific plan constitutes a psychiatric emergency requiring immediate and aggressive management. [7] [8]

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Introduction
content: An estimated 90% of individuals who complete suicide have a psychiatric disorder, most commonly a mood disorder. Recognizing suicidal ideation in these patients provides a critical opportunity for comprehensive evaluation of their challenges, needs, and risk levels. [9] Research indicates that 80% of suicide victims had consulted primary care clinicians within 1 year of death, but only 25% to 30% had seen psychiatric clinicians during the same period. [10] [11] Therefore, primary care clinicians are uniquely positioned to identify patients with suicidal ideation, assess suicide risk, and implement timely, appropriate interventions.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Etiology
content: Suicide arises from a combination of risk factors accumulated throughout life, with individual psychiatric disorders exerting the most significant influence on suicide rates. Conditions such as depression, bipolar disorder (BPD), schizophrenia-spectrum disorders, substance use disorders, epilepsy, and traumatic brain injury increase suicide risk by more than 3-fold. Although risk factors for suicide are well-established, the same level of certainty does not extend to suicidal ideation. A 2017 meta-analysis identified suicidal ideation as the 3rd strongest predictor of future suicide deaths, following prior psychiatric hospitalizations and suicide attempts. Past episodes of suicidal ideation are the most prominent risk factor for subsequent ideation, highlighting its persistent nature.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Etiology
content: In the U.S., the CDC reported that approximately 35 suicide attempts occurred for every completed adult suicide in 2021. For each suicide attempt, 2 adults had suicidal plans, and 7 adults reported suicidal thoughts. These statistics likely underestimate the true burden, as some suicides are misclassified as accidental deaths, and suicidal ideation is frequently underreported due to stigma. [12] [13] These data emphasize the importance of identifying individuals with suicidal ideation and understanding their trajectory toward suicide attempts.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Epidemiology
content: Suicide represents a significant public health issue worldwide. Data from the World Health Organization indicate that over 800,000 individuals die by suicide globally every year. Suicide is identified as the 18th leading cause of mortality overall and the 2nd leading cause among individuals aged 15 to 29 years. The frequency of suicide deaths is alarmingly high, with 1 occurring approximately every 40 seconds.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Epidemiology
content: Many countries experience substantial suicide rates. Between 1950 and 1995, global suicide rates increased by roughly 35% in men and 10% in women, affecting all age groups. [14] Actual suicide rates may be underreported, as deaths by suicide are often misclassified as “unnatural” or “undetermined,” potentially leading to underestimations. [15] [16] True rates could be 10% to 50% higher than reported, and nonfatal suicide attempts are estimated at 10 to 20 times the number of suicide deaths, with adolescents demonstrating a higher attempt-to-death ratio. [17] [18] Suicidal ideation without subsequent action is more prevalent than actual suicidal behavior.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Epidemiology
content: In the U.S., the CDC reported that from 1999 to 2017, the age-adjusted suicide rate increased by 33%, rising from 10.5 to 14.0 per 100,000 individuals. [19] A slight decrease occurred in 2019, from 14.2 per 100,000 population in 2018 to 13.9 per 100,000, but the rate rose again to 14.1 per 100,000 in 2021. Underestimation is a concern in the U.S., as many deaths may be misclassified, indicating that actual rates could be higher. [20]

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Pathophysiology
content: Suicidal ideation arises from complex interactions among psychological, biological, environmental, and cultural factors. The progression from ideation to suicidal behavior may be conceptualized using several theoretical frameworks, discussed below.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Pathophysiology -- Psychological Theories
content: Psychological theories of suicide emphasize the mental and behavioral processes that contribute to suicidal thoughts and actions. These models focus on how cognitive patterns, emotional responses, interpersonal experiences, and personality traits influence the emergence and progression of suicidal ideation.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Pathophysiology -- Stress-diathesis models
content: Diathesis denotes an individual’s predisposition to suicidal behavior, shaped by genetic, biological, and psychological factors, including previous occurrences of mental health disorders, personality traits, or past trauma. This model proposes that suicidal ideation may emerge when such individuals encounter stressful life events exceeding their coping capacity. Traits such as impulsivity and aggression further increase the likelihood of acting on these thoughts. [21]

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Pathophysiology -- Ideation-to-action framework
content: The ideation-to-action framework emphasizes understanding how individuals progress from contemplating suicide to attempting such an act, recognizing that suicidal thoughts and attempts are related yet distinct behaviors. A critical factor in this transition is an individual’s capability for suicide, which encompasses multiple elements that enable the execution of a suicide attempt. Several psychological theories employ this framework to explain suicidal behavior.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Pathophysiology -- Ideation-to-action framework
content: The interpersonal theory of suicide highlights acquired capability as a key determinant in the progression from suicidal ideation to attempts. Acquired capability involves a reduced fear of death and increased tolerance for physical pain, often resulting from repeated exposure to painful or distressing experiences, such as childhood trauma or combat. Individuals with elevated acquired capability are more likely to transition from ideation to suicide attempts.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Pathophysiology -- Ideation-to-action framework
content: The integrated motivational-volitional model offers a comprehensive perspective on suicidal behavior, delineating 3 phases. The premotivational phase considers background factors and life events that may trigger suicidal thoughts. The motivational phase involves the development of ideation due to feelings of defeat, entrapment, and lack of social support.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Pathophysiology -- Ideation-to-action framework
content: The volitional phase focuses on the transition from ideation to action, with volitional moderators, including access to means, exposure to suicidal behavior, reduced fear of death, increased pain tolerance, impulsivity, planning, mental imagery, and a history of prior attempts, determining whether ideation progresses to an attempt. This model integrates psychological, biological, and social factors, providing a detailed framework for understanding the complex pathways leading to suicidal actions.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Pathophysiology -- Ideation-to-action framework
content: The 3-step theory of suicide describes the progression from suicidal ideation to suicidal behavior. According to this theory, the 1st step involves experiencing intense psychological pain and hopelessness, which prompts contemplation of suicide as a means of escape. The 2nd step involves feelings of social disconnection and perceiving oneself as a burden to others, amplifying initial distress. The 3rd step entails the development of a capability for suicide, characterized by overcoming the fear of death and acquiring the means to act on suicidal thoughts.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Pathophysiology -- Ideation-to-action framework
content: The fluid vulnerability theory proposes that an individual’s risk for suicide fluctuates over time, resulting from dynamic interactions between baseline factors, such as chronic or stable risk and protective elements, and acute factors, including reactions to external stressors. The concept of a "suicidal mode" reflects the interplay of chronic factors, such as sex, trauma, psychiatric history, and prior suicide attempts, with acute factors, including emotional distress and adverse life events. These interactions influence cognition, behavior, physiology, and emotion.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Pathophysiology -- Biological Theories
content: Biological theories of suicide focus on the neurobiological, genetic, and physiological mechanisms that influence the emergence of suicidal ideation and behavior. These models explore how dysregulation in stress-response systems, neuroinflammatory processes, and genetic predispositions contribute to vulnerability for suicidal thoughts and actions.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Pathophysiology -- Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis dysfunction
content: Dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, a central component of the stress response, is increasingly associated with mental health disorders, particularly suicidal ideation. [28] This axis, comprising a hormonal cascade from the hypothalamus to the pituitary and adrenal glands, regulates cortisol release. Disruptions in the HPA axis, potentially influenced by epigenetic factors such as early life trauma or gene variants (eg, FKBP5 affecting glucocorticoid receptor sensitivity), can produce imbalances in cortisol secretion. [29]

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Pathophysiology -- Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis dysfunction
content: Research examining HPA axis dysfunction in suicidal ideation demonstrates heterogeneous findings, reflecting differing cortisol responses across subgroups. For example, acute suicidal ideation may correlate with elevated cortisol, whereas a family history of suicide or prior attempts has been linked to attenuated cortisol responses under stress. These observations underscore the complex and multifaceted role of HPA axis dysregulation in suicidal ideation. [30]

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Pathophysiology -- Neuroinflammation and immune system dysfunction
content: Increased microglial density and activation have been associated with suicidal ideation, as demonstrated by postmortem studies and in vivo positron emission tomography scans. [31] This activation influences the tryptophan-kynurenine pathway, leading to elevated neurotoxic compounds such as quinolinic acid, which disrupt glutamate neurotransmission. Dysregulation of this pathway has been linked to neuropsychiatric disorders and suicidality. [32] Modulating enzymes within the tryptophan-kynurenine pathway has been proposed as a therapeutic approach for depression and suicidal ideation. [33] Elevated translocator protein levels, indicative of neuroinflammation, have been observed in patients with depression, particularly those experiencing suicidal ideation. [34]

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Pathophysiology -- Genetic factors
content: Genetic studies have focused on FKBP5 gene variants, which have been implicated in both depression and suicidal ideation. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses indicate that these variants are associated with increased susceptibility to depressive disorders and suicidality, supporting a role for genetic predisposition. [37]

title: Suicidal Ideation -- History and Physical
content: The history and physical examination of patients with suicidal ideation constitute essential components of a comprehensive psychiatric assessment. These evaluations aim to identify contributing factors, assess immediate risk, and guide appropriate therapeutic interventions.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- History and Physical -- Screening for Suicidal Ideation
content: Assessment of suicidal ideation and suicide risk is critical in both mental health and primary care settings. No single tool or method exists to determine an individual’s risk level definitively. Clinicians should employ a combination of evaluation strategies, including clinical interviews and validated self-report measures. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force emphasizes that routine screening alone does not significantly reduce suicide attempts or suicide-related mortality among adolescents, adults, or older adults. These findings highlight the limitations of existing tools and underscore the necessity of comprehensive, multifaceted patient evaluations. Evidence indicates that asking about suicide does not increase suicidal ideation or behavior. [38]

title: Suicidal Ideation -- History and Physical -- Risk Factors for Suicide
content: Certain populations demonstrate elevated suicide rates, including older adults, men, and members of the LGBTQ (lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer) community. [39] Risk factors are classified as predisposing, such as neuropsychiatric disorders, family history of suicide, past suicide attempts, adverse childhood experiences, and socioeconomic challenges, and precipitating, including substance use disorders, access to lethal means, stressful life events, and recent diagnoses of terminal or chronic illness. These factors may heighten feelings of isolation, hopelessness, and perceived burdensomeness. Media influence has also been noted, although its direct correlation with suicide deaths remains relatively weak. A thorough clinical history of patients with suicidal ideation should comprehensively explore these risk factors.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- History and Physical -- Psychiatric Evaluation in Suicide Risk Assessment
content: Assessment of suicide risk requires a thorough psychiatric evaluation that considers multiple factors, including current suicidal ideation, history of suicide attempts, existing psychiatric disorders—such as depression, schizophrenia, substance use disorders, anxiety, borderline personality disorder, and adjustment disorders—psychiatric symptoms, prior psychiatric hospitalizations, and recent biopsychosocial stressors. Evaluating access to firearms and protective factors, particularly those related to reasons for living, is also important, despite limited evidence supporting their impact.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- History and Physical -- Psychiatric Evaluation in Suicide Risk Assessment
content: Substance use, especially involving alcohol, substantially increases suicide risk, with heightened vulnerability when comorbid with disorders such as BPD or depression, often due to associated impulsivity and aggression. A comprehensive evaluation should additionally incorporate the patient’s psychiatric history, past and current treatments, family history of psychiatric disorders, coping strategies, and collateral information from friends, family, or treatment records.

content: Risk stratification constitutes an important component of suicide risk assessment. However, current evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the use of formal risk scoring systems due to methodological limitations and inconsistent findings. title: Suicidal Ideation -- History and Physical -- Assessment of Suicidal Ideations
content: Assessment of suicidal ideation requires a comprehensive clinical evaluation encompassing multiple key domains. A detailed characterization of suicidal thoughts is essential, including onset, frequency, duration, intensity, triggers, associated factors, perceived control over these thoughts, attribution, and whether the ideation is passive or active. This information provides critical insight into the severity and immediacy of risk. Differentiating between passive and active suicidal ideation helps identify short-term risks, although suicide attempts can occur without prior expression of ideation, and long-term risk appears comparable for both types.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- History and Physical -- Assessment of Suicidal Ideations
content: Evaluation of a suicide plan is particularly important, as the presence and specificity of a plan strongly correlate with the likelihood of a serious attempt. Assessing access to lethal means is crucial, given that increased availability elevates the risk of fatal outcomes. Determining the patient’s intent to die is vital, as any degree of intent constitutes affirmation of suicidal intent. Appraisal of the lethality of the method should consider both the clinician’s assessment and the patient’s perception of lethality. Identification of protective factors, such as relationships or circumstances that motivate continued living, informs potential interventions. Inquiry into previous suicide attempts, including aborted or interrupted attempts, is essential, as a history of such behavior significantly increases the risk of future attempts.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Evaluation
content: Suicide risk assessment scales offer structured instruments for clinicians to systematically evaluate the severity of suicidal ideation and inform decisions regarding appropriate interventions, thereby improving the precision and effectiveness of suicide prevention efforts. Several scales are available to assess suicidal ideation severity and estimate suicide risk, with the most commonly utilized outlined below.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Evaluation
content: The Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale is frequently used to evaluate the severity and immediacy of suicidal thoughts, suicide attempt behaviors, and the lethality of attempts. This scale effectively identifies individuals requiring urgent intervention and is applied extensively in both clinical and research settings. The Beck Scale for Suicide Ideation, created by Dr. Aaron T. Beck, measures the intensity of suicidal thoughts using 21 items that capture multiple dimensions of ideation. This evaluation tool is particularly useful in clinical practice for identifying at-risk individuals and monitoring changes in suicidal ideation, with higher scores reflecting increased severity.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Evaluation
content: The Suicidal Ideation Attributes Scale assesses the presence and intensity of suicidal thoughts, primarily in community populations. Comprising 5 items, the scale evaluates factors such as frequency, controllability, distress, and functional impact, with higher scores on the 10-point scale indicating greater severity. The Patient Health Questionnaire-9 serves as a brief screening tool commonly incorporated into medical records. The 9th item of this assessment tool, which addresses thoughts of death or self-harm, is critical for identifying patients at elevated suicide risk, making this questionnaire an essential instrument across diverse clinical settings. title: Suicidal Ideation -- Treatment / Management -- Nonpharmacological Treatment
content: Psychotherapeutic interventions for suicide prevention focus on modifying maladaptive thought patterns, emotional regulation, and coping strategies. These methods aim to reduce self-directed violence through skills development and structured behavioral approaches.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Treatment / Management -- Nonpharmacological Treatment
content: Techniques adapted from cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) are strongly recommended for patients with a recent history of self-directed violence to reduce the risk of future incidents. Studies utilizing CBT have directly addressed suicide risk, and systematic reviews and meta-analyses have examined its effects on suicide-related outcomes. Patient satisfaction with CBT focused on suicide prevention is generally high, and the quality of evidence supporting these benefits is considered moderate.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Treatment / Management -- Nonpharmacological Treatment
content: Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) is indicated for individuals with borderline personality disorder who have recently engaged in self-directed violence. Incorporating elements of CBT, skills training, and mindfulness techniques, DBT aims to enhance emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness, and distress tolerance. Research supports the efficacy of DBT in reducing both nonsuicidal and suicidal self-directed violence among patients with borderline personality disorder, although the quality of evidence is low.

content: Crisis response plans are recommended for individuals with suicidal ideation or known suicide attempts. Evidence indicates that such plans can reduce suicide attempts among military personnel who experience acute suicidal ideation or have a history of attempts. The overall quality of evidence is low, and certain study limitations exist.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Treatment / Management -- Nonpharmacological Treatment
content: Problem-solving-based therapies are suggested for patients with a history of self-directed violence or feelings of hopelessness, particularly those with moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury. title: Suicidal Ideation -- Treatment / Management -- Pharmacological Therapies
content: Medications play a critical role in suicide prevention by addressing psychiatric disorders and neurobiological factors that increase the risk of self-directed violence. Pharmacological interventions can reduce the intensity of suicidal ideation, improve emotional regulation, and support long-term mental health management.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Treatment / Management -- Antidepressants
content: Antidepressants have demonstrated efficacy in reducing suicidal ideation and behavior. A recent systematic review found that 9 of 12 studies specifically examining suicidal thoughts reported reductions associated with antidepressant use. Additionally, a meta-analysis conducted by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) indicated that antidepressants decrease the risk of suicidal behavior in older adults. Further pharmacoepidemiological research has shown that selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are effective in reducing suicidal behavior across broader populations, including young adults. These medications carry an FDA black box warning for increased suicidal risk in children and adolescents, highlighting the necessity for careful monitoring for medication-induced suicidality.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Treatment / Management -- Ketamine
content: Ketamine has been shown to produce rapid reductions in suicidal ideation, with effectiveness observed following a single intravenous dose of 0.5 mg/kg. While the clinical practice guidelines of the Veterans Affairs and the Department of Defense support the use of this noncompetitive N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonist, the evidence is limited by small trial populations, resulting in predominantly off-label application for suicidal behavior. At this dosage, ketamine is generally well tolerated, with adverse effects including sedation, depersonalization or derealization, nausea, dizziness, and agitation. In August 2020, the FDA approved intranasal esketamine for addressing depressive symptoms in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) who exhibit acute suicidal ideation and behavior.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Treatment / Management -- Lithium
content: Lithium is recommended for patients with mood disorders, particularly BPD, to reduce the risk of suicide. Maintenance therapy with lithium has been associated with fewer suicidal behaviors and deaths in individuals with unipolar depression or BPD. Prescribing considerations include patient preference and adherence challenges due to adverse effects. Long-term lithium use can produce a greater decline in glomerular filtration rate than aging alone, with an average 30% reduction observed over an 18-year treatment period. Significant kidney function impairment typically emerges after 6 to 10 years of therapy, and approximately 18.1% of users develop stage 3 chronic kidney disease after 30 years.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Treatment / Management -- Lithium
content: Risk factors include prolonged treatment duration, elevated serum lithium levels, older age, and comorbid conditions. No specific interventions exist for lithium-induced renal dysfunction. However, maintaining serum levels between 0.4 and 0.6 mEq/L is recommended to reduce risk, with lower doses remaining effective for relapse prevention.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Treatment / Management -- Clozapine
content: Clozapine is indicated for patients with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder who exhibit suicidal ideation or a history of suicide attempts. Evidence indicates that clozapine reduces suicidal behaviors in this population. The quality of evidence for reducing actual suicide attempts or completed suicide is low, and side effects and intensive monitoring requirements limit the use of this agent. FDA guidelines mandate weekly monitoring of absolute neutrophil count during the first 6 months of treatment. If counts remain at least 1,500/µL (or ≥1,000/µL for benign ethnic neutropenia), monitoring may be extended to every 2 weeks for the subsequent 6 months and monthly thereafter. title: Suicidal Ideation -- Treatment / Management -- Brain Stimulation Methods
content: Brain stimulation methods, encompassing interventions such as electroconvulsive therapy and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, show promise in reducing suicidal ideation. However, sample sizes in existing studies are insufficient to evaluate the impact of these interventions on actual suicide attempts. Similarly, deep brain stimulation has not yet demonstrated efficacy in preventing suicide attempts.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Treatment / Management -- Lethal Means Safety Measures
content: Lethal means safety measures, such as enforcing firearm restrictions, limiting access to toxic substances and medications, and installing barriers at high-risk locations, effectively reduce suicide incidence. Firearms represent a major risk factor, accounting for approximately half of suicides in the U.S., with most firearm suicide attempts proving fatal. Suicide rates correlate with state firearm laws and ownership levels. Firearms are frequently used among military personnel and veterans, prompting strategies to sequester weapons from at-risk individuals.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Treatment / Management -- Lethal Means Safety Measures
content: Safety counseling emphasizes secure storage or transfer of firearms to authorized persons. Restricting access to opioids, limiting paracetamol pack sizes, and controlling pesticide availability, as demonstrated in Sri Lanka and India, are associated with reductions in suicide and accidental poisoning. Barriers at lethal heights decrease jumping suicides, although displacement to nearby sites without barriers can occur.

content: Public health strategies have long targeted community-based suicide prevention interventions. Constraints include inadequate control of confounders and uncertainty regarding the balance between benefits and harms.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnosis for suicidal ideation encompasses a broad spectrum of psychiatric, psychological, and medical conditions that may contribute to or coexist with these thoughts. Thus, a thorough evaluation is essential for accurate assessment and effective intervention.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Mood disorders, including MDD, BPD in both manic and depressive phases, and dysthymia, are strongly associated with suicidal ideation. Disorders characterized by anxiety, such as generalized anxiety disorder, posttraumatic stress disorder, panic disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder, can also contribute to these thoughts. Personality disorders, particularly BPD and antisocial personality disorder, are linked to impulsivity and self-harm behaviors. Psychotic disorders, including schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder, may influence suicidal ideation through delusions or hallucinations. Substance use disorders, involving alcohol or illicit drugs, can exacerbate psychiatric conditions or directly affect mood, cognition, and impulse control, increasing suicide risk.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Adjustment disorders arising from difficulty coping with major life changes or stressors may precipitate suicidal thoughts. Neurocognitive disorders, such as dementias, can present with depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation, while chronic medical conditions, especially those associated with pain, disability, or terminal illness, further elevate risk. Pathological eating behaviors, such as in anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa, frequently involve severe psychological distress and suicidal ideation. Previous childhood trauma, abuse, or neglect may lead to long-term psychological consequences, including suicidal thoughts. Additionally, acute situational stressors, such as relationship conflicts, financial strain, or legal issues, can precipitate suicidal ideation, particularly when coping resources or social support are inadequate.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Pertinent Studies and Ongoing Trials
content: The 2019 FDA approval of esketamine for adults with treatment-resistant MDD allows certain patients with coexisting suicidal intent to qualify for this therapy. Investigators are actively assessing whether ketamine produces a measurable and clinically significant reduction in suicidal intent, while also exploring alternative doses and routes of administration. Most completed studies have employed an intravenous ketamine infusion of 0.5 mg/kg delivered over 40 minutes in individuals with treatment-resistant MDD exhibiting varying severities of suicidal intent. Fewer studies have evaluated ketamine administered via oral, intramuscular, or intranasal routes. [58] Currently, randomized clinical trials are recruiting participants with suicidal thoughts to examine the efficacy of intranasal and oral ketamine administration.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis of suicidal ideation varies widely and depends on multiple factors, including the underlying causes of ideation, the presence and severity of mental health disorders, treatment effectiveness, and the individual’s support system. Prognosis is generally more favorable when suicidal ideation is linked to situational stressors that may be resolved, whereas ideation associated with chronic mental health disorders, such as MDD or BPD, depends on disorder severity and treatment response. Timely and appropriate psychiatric care, including psychotherapy, pharmacotherapy, or a combination, is associated with improved outcomes.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Prognosis
content: A robust support system comprising family, friends, healthcare professionals, and community resources further enhances prognosis. Conversely, risk factors such as prior suicide attempts, substance use, chronic physical illness, lack of support, and comorbid psychiatric conditions may worsen outcomes. Continuous suicide risk assessment and management, alongside the development of resilience and effective coping strategies, can improve prognosis. With prompt intervention and adequate support, many patients achieve meaningful symptom improvement and enhanced quality of life.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Complications
content: If not appropriately addressed, suicidal ideation may result in a range of complications affecting both the individual and their social network. These consequences may be psychological, physical, social, or a combination thereof. The most severe outcome is the progression to suicide attempts or completed suicide. Persistent suicidal thoughts can exacerbate preexisting mental health disorders, such as depression, anxiety, or posttraumatic stress disorder, leading to further deterioration of psychological well-being. Daily functioning may be impaired, with difficulties performing routine tasks, maintaining employment, or attending educational activities. Suicidal ideation often contributes to social withdrawal and isolation, which can intensify feelings of loneliness and despair.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Complications
content: Some individuals may engage in substance use to cope with distressing thoughts, increasing the risk of addiction and worsening mental health conditions. Chronic stress associated with suicidal ideation may also contribute to physical health problems, including cardiovascular dysfunction, impaired immune response, and gastrointestinal disturbances. Interpersonal relationships may be strained, with conflicts, communication breakdowns, and loss of support networks. Stigma and discrimination can hinder affected individuals from seeking help, further exacerbating isolation and psychological distress. Suicidal behaviors may also result in legal or financial difficulties, particularly if injury or prolonged medical care is required. Additionally, family members and close associates may experience significant emotional trauma, which can adversely affect their mental health.

content: Psychiatric consultation is often indicated to complete the suicide risk assessment and establish an appropriate treatment regimen. Psychological testing may be warranted. Services such as social work and occupational therapy may be involved in care planning to address modifiable risk factors.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Counseling patients and families to restrict access to lethal means, such as locking medications or removing or securing firearms, during episodes of suicidal ideation is recommended in the literature. However, chart reviews indicate that this counseling is often not implemented. A training intervention for healthcare professionals working in the emergency department improved the frequency with which counseling regarding lethal means was initiated. [59] Patients may not receive counseling in emergency departments if nurses do not have a designated counselor available, as nurses often hesitate to be confrontational. [60] Further research and formal guidelines are needed to determine the most effective techniques for patient education and counseling.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: School-based educational programs may reduce suicidal ideation, but a recent systematic review found the quality of evidence to be low. Currently, evidence is insufficient to support the effectiveness of gatekeeper training programs. [61] A project in rural India trained laypersons within their communities to improve the detection and treatment of mental health issues. Additionally, community education successfully reduced stigma surrounding mental illness in these rural populations. [62]

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Similar approaches may be effective for high-risk groups. For example, a systematic review demonstrated that individuals coping with the death of a loved one by suicide exhibit high rates of suicidal intent, ranging from 15% to 49%. [63] Education aimed at reducing stigma and fear of appearing weak or unfit for duty may improve reporting of suicidal intent among populations with high rates of suicidality who typically avoid disclosure. [64] [65] A best-practice intervention involves assisting patients in formulating a safety plan that incorporates appropriate support, resources, distractions, and safeguards to prevent access to lethal means.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Healthcare professionals, including physicians, advanced care practitioners, nurses, and pharmacists, should integrate specialized skills, strategic planning, ethical considerations, clearly defined responsibilities, effective communication, and coordinated care when treating patients with suicidal ideation and at risk of self-harm. This collaborative approach optimizes patient outcomes, ensures safety, and enhances overall team performance.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Physicians and advanced care practitioners must be proficient in conducting comprehensive psychiatric evaluations and risk assessments, which are essential for determining the severity and immediacy of suicide risk. Nurses provide continuous monitoring, observe behavioral changes, and support adherence to treatment plans. Pharmacists contribute by managing medication regimens, advising on appropriate dosages, and monitoring for potential adverse effects or interactions.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Strategically, management should involve a comprehensive plan addressing biological, psychological, cultural, social, and spiritual dimensions of care. An interprofessional approach ensures that each team member’s expertise is applied effectively to create a holistic care plan. Clearly delineating roles within the team is critical to prevent overlaps or gaps in care, with each member understanding their responsibilities and contributions to managing the patient’s suicidality. Ethically, upholding patient autonomy and securing informed consent are essential. Patients should actively participate in care decisions and be thoroughly informed regarding the risks and benefits associated with various treatment options. This patient-centered approach preserves dignity and fosters engagement and adherence to treatment.

title: Suicidal Ideation -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Effective interprofessional communication is crucial to ensure that every team member is aware of the patient’s current status, treatment plan, and any changes in condition. Regular team meetings, shared electronic health records, and open communication channels facilitate this process. Care coordination is particularly important during transitions between levels of care or healthcare settings. Sharing accurate information promptly with the patient and care team supports ongoing care, helps prevent relapse, and strengthens crisis response. Collaborative, patient-centered care strengthens outcomes and safety while improving the cohesion and effectiveness of the interprofessional team treating patients at risk of self-harm.
